results.summary: This design combines two independent circuits: a Fibonacci sequence calculator using 56-bit integers and a Gold code generator for CCSDS X-band PN Delta-DOR. The Fibonacci terms are displayed one hex character at a time on the 7-segment display, with the decimal point marking the least significant bit. The Gold code generator uses LFSRs and allows parallel loading of 6 bits to select different sequences; the display dot shows either the Fibonacci output or the Gold code output based on an input select. The design is tested manually by driving the clock and setting the appropriate inputs; no external hardware is required.

This is a pseudo-random number generator based on a 16-bit Fibonacci linear-feedback shift register. It produces one new random bit per clock cycle, with the last 8 bits available on the output pins, and supports loading a custom seed value via the data_in pin when load_en is high. The design is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested by manually clocking the circuit and observing the output on a hex display. No external hardware is needed.

This design implements an LED chaser on a 7-segment display. A shift register is used to sequentially light up segments, with the input controlled by a push button. When the button is pressed, the illuminated segment shifts, creating a chasing effect. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires no external hardware.

This chip performs conversions and comparisons between binary-encoded ternary and unary-encoded ternary, with both machine-readable and human-readable outputs. It supports four operation modes selected by opcodes, and outputs results either on a 7-segment display or as binary signals. The design is implemented using mixed radix circuit synthesis (MRCS) and Wokwi, and it can be tested by setting the mode and input pins to verify the conversion or comparison. No external hardware is required.

This design is a counter that displays its count on a 7-segment display or allows manual entry of a number in binary. It includes a clock divider to slow down the counting speed, and the counter can be enabled or disabled. The design is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested by enabling the counter and clock divider to observe counting, or by disabling the counter and setting the inputs to display a specific number. No external hardware is needed.

This design is a clock divider implemented using a series of flip-flops. The documentation is minimal, with only the title and a brief description, and no testing instructions are provided. It is implemented in Wokwi and uses a 7-segment display for output, but the exact functionality and usage are not described. No external hardware is mentioned.

This chip is a scalable synchronous 4-bit tri-directional loadable counter that can count up, down, or pause, and supports loading a new count value. It is intended to be usable as a program counter, for example to set the next address for a jump instruction. The design is implemented using mixed radix circuit synthesis (MRCS) and Wokwi, and it can be tested by resetting the state, setting the direction and count enable, and clocking the circuit. No external hardware is needed.

This design replicates the functionality of TI's 74xx1G97 and 74xx1G98 configurable logic gates, along with a 74xx1G79 D flip-flop. It includes two configurable gates and one D flip-flop, each with complementary outputs. The design is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested by referring to the TI datasheets for the original parts. No external hardware is required beyond the standard Tiny Tapeout setup.

This design implements a 4-digit electronic padlock that checks a sequence of button presses against a stored code. Each button press is detected by a rising edge detector and the resulting binary code is stored in a shift register, which is continuously compared to a reference value. The design outputs signals indicating button press detection and code validity. It requires external push buttons with debounce circuitry and a clock source.

This design drives a 7-segment LED display to alternate between the text 'NIC' and 'JAC'. It uses a prescaler with selectable tap points to divide the clock, which then feeds a ripple counter and a chain of multiplexers to control each segment. The decimal point blinks based on the highest counter bit. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires external switches for prescaler selection and a 7-segment display.
